messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 40
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Data Scientist
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 64

**Patient Vignette: Data Scientist, Age 40**

She sits in the chair with her back straight, hands folded in her lap, her posture a perfect mirror of the spreadsheets she manages at work. She is a data scientist, a woman whose life is built on patterns, on cleaning messy datasets until they reveal a clean, linear truth. She tells me this in our first session, almost apologetically, as if to warn me that her own story might not be so tidy.

The trauma happened eighteen months ago. She was at a coffee shop near her office, a Tuesday morning, waiting for a latte. She remembers the exact sound of the steam wand hissing, the smell of roasted beans, the specific shade of blue of the barista’s apron. Then, a man at a table near the window stood up, screamed something she couldn’t understand, and pulled a knife from his jacket. He didn't attack anyone. He turned the knife on himself. She watched him fall. She saw the blood spread across the tile floor, a shocking, bright red against the gray and white. She was not the target. She was not harmed. She was simply there.

In the weeks that followed, she told herself it was a terrible thing to see, but it was over. She had no physical wounds. She went back to work the next day. She ran her algorithms. She cleaned her data. She told her husband she was fine. But the data in her own mind began to corrupt.

The first pattern she noticed was a shift in her environment. The coffee shop is now a dead zone. She cannot walk past it. The smell of coffee, once a comfort, now triggers a spike of adrenaline so sharp she feels nauseous. At the grocery store, the sound of a dropped jar of pasta sauce sends her heart into a sprint, her hands trembling as she abandons her cart. She has become a hyper-vigilant scanner of human faces, looking for the tell—the flicker of agitation, the tightening of a jaw—that precedes an explosion. She sees the man’s face in every crowd, a ghost in the machine.

Her work, once her sanctuary of logic, has become a minefield. She cannot concentrate on a single line of code. She will stare at a screen for an hour, the numbers swimming, while her mind replays the sound of the knife clattering on the tile. She has started to avoid the open-plan office, working from home, which her manager accepts because her output is still technically above average. But it takes her three times as long. She feels a constant, low-grade exhaustion, as if she is running a marathon in her sleep.

The most painful pattern is in her marriage. Her husband is patient, but she can see the confusion in his eyes. He reaches for her at night, and she flinches. Not because of him, but because the touch feels like an intrusion, a threat. She has stopped wanting sex. She has stopped wanting to be touched at all. She sleeps on the far edge of the bed, her body coiled, listening. She feels a deep, irrational guilt. She tells herself that other people have real trauma, real loss. She just *saw* something. She has no right to be this broken. She tries to logic her way out of it, but the logic fails. The data doesn’t lie.

Last week, she was driving home when a motorcycle backfired. She slammed on the brakes in the middle of an intersection, her hands locked on the wheel, her vision tunneling. She sat there for a full minute, unable to move, as cars honked around her. She didn’t see the road. She saw the tile floor. She saw the red. When she finally got home, she didn’t tell her husband. She went straight to the bathroom, sat on the cold floor, and cried for the first time in a year. She didn’t know why she was crying. She only knew that the clean, linear truth she had built her life on had been replaced by a noise she could not filter out.
